name: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species

clinicalPearls: The pseudomonads are a heterogeneous group of non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacteria now split across three medically important genera: Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas; most cause disease opportunistically, the exceptions being the primary pathogens B. pseudomallei and B. mallei.

P. aeruginosa rarely causes infection without a breach in host defenses; disease typically requires compromised immunity, mucosal trauma, physiologic derangement, or antibiotic-mediated suppression of normal flora, so most infections cluster in intensive care units.

On primary culture P. aeruginosa is identified by a yellow to dark-green or bluish pigment, a shiny gun-metal colony sheen, a characteristic fruity odor, failure to ferment lactose on MacConkey agar, and a positive oxidase reaction; cystic fibrosis isolates may appear mucoid from overproduction of alginate.

Ecthyma gangrenosum is the distinctive skin lesion of P. aeruginosa bacteremia, occurring almost exclusively in markedly neutropenic patients and those with AIDS; lesions begin pink, darken to purple, then become black and necrotic, and histologically are due to vascular invasion teeming with bacteria.

P. aeruginosa keratitis is a medical emergency because it can progress over roughly 48 hours to involve the entire cornea with opacification and even perforation; it is strongly associated with contact lenses, especially the extended-wear type.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa most often occurs in elderly diabetics and can extend to cranial nerve palsies (most commonly cranial nerve VII) or cavernous sinus thrombosis; the ESR is invariably elevated, often 100 mm/h or more.

Hot-tub folliculitis, toe-web infection, and the green-nail syndrome (pyocyanin diffusing into the nail bed of a Pseudomonas paronychia) are characteristic community skin manifestations; whirlpools, spas, and pools are common sources, and folliculitis is usually self-limited.

Vertebral osteomyelitis and sternoclavicular septic arthritis are uncommon but characteristic complications in people who inject drugs; Pseudomonas osteomyelitis of the foot typically follows a puncture wound through a sneaker, mainly in children, often with negative blood cultures.

Melioidosis (B. pseudomallei) is geographically restricted chiefly to Southeast Asia and northern Australia (with cases in India and China); the organism is a facultative intracellular pathogen acquired from soil and water that can cause latent infection presenting long after exposure.

Melioidosis can mimic tuberculosis with chronic cough, fever, hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary upper-lobe disease, and may also present as skin ulceration with lymphangitis and regional lymphadenopathy or as high-mortality septicemia.

Burkholderia cepacia complex can cause the rapidly fatal cepacia syndrome (respiratory distress plus septicemia) in cystic fibrosis; B. cenocepacia in particular is a barrier to lung transplantation, with relatively high one-year mortality.

Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an opportunist whose emergence requires major disruption of host flora, classically broad-spectrum cephalosporin or carbapenem therapy; distinguishing colonization from true infection in ventilated, non-neutropenic patients is a recurring clinical dilemma.
harrison.pathophysiology: P. aeruginosa possesses an unusually large arsenal of putative virulence factors, yet few are individually proven to drive human disease, and there is great redundancy. Adhesins (pili, flagellin/flagellar cap binding mucins, LPS outer core binding CFTR to aid internalization, and alginate in mucoid strains) mediate colonization, with adhesion strongest to injured cell surfaces. A type III secretion system injects toxins (ExoS or ExoU, ExoT, ExoY) into host cells, allowing evasion of phagocytes; strains secreting ExoU are associated with higher mortality. A type II secretion system releases diffusible toxins including exotoxin A, multiple proteases (which degrade host cytokines and chemokines), and phospholipases. Rhamnolipids, pyocyanin, and hydrocyanic acid further injure tissue and can cause neutrophil death. Inflammatory responses to lipid A and flagellin via Toll-like receptors (principally TLR4 and TLR5) are required for defense but, when florid, contribute to sepsis and septic shock. In chronic infection (cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, diffuse panbronchiolitis) defective mucociliary clearance and mucus stasis select for P. aeruginosa, which adapts over time by losing pili and flagella, losing the O side chain of LPS (becoming complement-sensitive), and overproducing mucoid exopolysaccharide, dampening the host response and enabling decades of persistence with attenuated virulence factor production. B. pseudomallei survives within neutrophils and macrophages, aided by a polysaccharide capsule and a type III secretion system, and provokes a florid inflammatory response. B. cepacia complex organisms bind lung mucus and possess potent LPS that drives lung inflammation. S. maltophilia virulence is limited, with disease largely a host inflammatory response to LPS and flagellin; its hallmark is broad intrinsic antibiotic resistance via efflux pumps and the L1 and L2 beta-lactamases.
additionalDifferentials: Other gram-negative bacterial pneumonia and sepsis (clinically often indistinguishable from P. aeruginosa)
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (can also produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions)
Pyogenic meningitis of other bacterial etiology (CSF profile of Pseudomonas meningitis is nonspecific)
Polymicrobial osteomyelitis from trauma or decubitus ulcers
infectionMimics: Aspergillosis and mucormycosis (can produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions)
Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species causing malignant/necrotizing otitis externa
Tuberculosis mimicked by chronic pulmonary melioidosis
Other gram-negative enterocolitis mimicked by Pseudomonas enterocolitis / Shanghai fever
nonInfectiousMimics: Fluid overload mistaken for pneumonia on CT in ventilated patients (contributes to overdiagnosis of HAP/VAP)
additionalInvestigations: Sputum Gram stain showing predominant polymorphonuclear leukocytes plus culture positive for P. aeruginosa supports acute pneumonia rather than colonization
Multiplex PCR platforms on respiratory and blood samples identify P. aeruginosa earlier than classical culture
Technetium-99 bone scan as the gold standard for malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa
MRI and bone scan for puncture-wound foot osteomyelitis; needle aspiration usually yields the diagnosis
Deep bone biopsy before treating presumed P. aeruginosa osteomyelitis in trauma or decubitus settings to confirm its causative role
Blood cultures plus echocardiographic/clinical signs for endocarditis (blood cultures often negative in vertebral osteomyelitis unless endocarditis coexists)
Mandatory laboratory susceptibility testing before using newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor agents or cefiderocol against MDR/XDR strains
redFlags: Ecthyma gangrenosum in a neutropenic or AIDS patient suggesting P. aeruginosa bacteremia
Rapidly progressive corneal opacification/perforation indicating sight-threatening Pseudomonas keratitis (medical emergency)
Severe lancinating ear pain with granulation tissue in a diabetic, plus cranial nerve palsy, signaling malignant otitis externa
Hypothermia or shock in P. aeruginosa bacteremia (marker of severe illness)
Cepacia syndrome: rapidly fatal respiratory distress with septicemia in cystic fibrosis
Hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary disease in a patient from an endemic region suggesting melioidosis with systemic spread
harrison.prognosis: P. aeruginosa carries high attributable mortality and is among the most feared pathogens in neutropenic patients. Historical crude bacteremia mortality exceeded 50%, with more recent attributable mortality of about 28 to 44% depending on adequacy and timing of treatment and underlying disease severity. Pneumonia mortality has been reported at 40 to 80%, though the fraction attributable to underlying disease is uncertain, and VAP outcomes are poor. Chronic airway infection (e.g., cystic fibrosis) is rarely eradicated and is the leading contributor to respiratory failure and death in CF. Pseudomonas endovascular infection in people who inject drugs is more indolent than S. aureus endocarditis and is more often curable when right-sided. Melioidosis septicemia carries high mortality, with rates as high as 44% reported in Thailand. B. cenocepacia infection has relatively high one-year mortality after lung transplantation. S. maltophilia pneumonia/bacteremia can cause septic shock, with a severe high-mortality form described in neutropenic patients.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing HAP/VAP: positive sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or PCR results may reflect tracheobronchial colonization, endotracheal-tube biofilm, or simple tracheobronchitis rather than true pneumonia; clinical judgment is essential.
In trauma- or decubitus-associated osteomyelitis, infection is often polymicrobial and the causative role of P. aeruginosa can be overstated without a deep bone biopsy.
Treating S. maltophilia or P. aeruginosa pulmonary cultures as infection when they may represent colonization, especially in non-neutropenic patients; unnecessary therapy promotes resistance.
Assuming community sputum cultures prove community-acquired P. aeruginosa pneumonia in patients prone to airway colonization by multiple bacterial strains.

Empirically relying on first-line antipseudomonal agents in settings where susceptibility is below 80%, or on the newer agents/cefiderocol without susceptibility testing given unpredictable resistance mechanisms.

Failing to remove indwelling foreign bodies (urinary catheters, stents, stones, central lines) — relapse of UTI or bacteremia may be due to the retained device or ongoing obstruction rather than antibiotic resistance.
Not recognizing that melioidosis can present long after travel to an endemic area due to latent intracellular infection.
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal severity score is presented. Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) P. aeruginosa, with extremely high MDR rates reported from eastern/southern Europe, Latin America, India, and China, especially in ICUs. Carbapenemase production is highlighted as the most threatening resistance mechanism. The B. cepacia cepacia syndrome denotes a rapidly fatal severe phenotype. Melioidosis spans a clinical spectrum from asymptomatic infection through localized abscesses and pneumonia to high-mortality disseminated septicemic disease.
management: Treat serious P. aeruginosa infection with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as an antipseudomonal penicillin, cephalosporin or carbapenem, guided by susceptibility given widespread resistance
Consider combination therapy adding an aminoglycoside or an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone in severe sepsis, neutropenia or high-resistance settings
Achieve source control, including debridement of ecthyma gangrenosum, drainage of collections and prolonged therapy for osteomyelitis and endocarditis
Manage malignant necrotising otitis externa with prolonged systemic antipseudomonal therapy and diabetic control, following the erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Treat Pseudomonas keratitis urgently with intensive topical antipseudomonal drops and contact-lens removal, as it is a sight-threatening emergency
Use trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as preferred therapy for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, recognising its intrinsic carbapenem resistance
Treat Burkholderia pseudomallei melioidosis with intravenous ceftazidime or a carbapenem followed by prolonged oral eradication therapy
Support neutropenic and critically ill patients and seek infectious-diseases advice given high attributable mortality
